If the amount of sodium to be delivered is a concern, such as when serum sodium levels exceed 145 mEq/L, consider using intravenous potassium phosphates to replenish phosphorus levels. Administering solutions containing both sodium and phosphorus in patients with impaired renal function may lead to hypernatremia or hyperphosphatemia. Lanthanum carbonate reduces the effectiveness of intravenous sodium phosphates by binding cations in the gastrointestinal tract. This interaction is contraindicated. Lanthanum carbonate decreases serum phosphate concentrations by binding dietary phosphate. Sevelamer also reduces the effectiveness of intravenous sodium phosphates through cation binding in the gastrointestinal tract. This interaction is contraindicated. Sevelamer decreases serum phosphate concentrations by binding dietary phosphate. Intravenous sodium phosphates can reduce the absorption and effectiveness of baloxavir marboxil due to cation binding in the gastrointestinal tract. Avoid co-administration or use an alternative drug. Baloxavir may bind to polyvalent cations, leading to decreased absorption. Studies in monkeys have shown that concurrent use with calcium, aluminum, or iron significantly reduces plasma levels. Human studies have not been conducted. Benazepril increases the toxicity of intravenous sodium phosphates through pharmacodynamic synergy. Avoid co-administration or use an alternative drug. ACE inhibitors may enhance the nephrotoxic effects of sodium phosphates. Captopril and intravenous sodium phosphates can mutually increase each other's toxicity through an unspecified interaction mechanism. Avoid co-administration or use an alternative drug. ACE inhibitors may enhance the nephrotoxic effects of sodium phosphates. Erdafitinib and intravenous sodium phosphates should not be co-administered during the initial dosing adjustment period (the first 21 days). Increases in serum phosphate levels are a pharmacodynamic effect of FGFR inhibition. Serum phosphate binders may obscure decisions regarding initial dosage adjustments. Calcium carbonate reduces the effectiveness of intravenous sodium phosphates by binding cations in the gastrointestinal tract. Modify therapy or monitor closely. Calcium decreases serum phosphate concentrations by binding dietary phosphate. Use alternatives if available. Calcium citrate also reduces the effectiveness of intravenous sodium phosphates through cation binding in the gastrointestinal tract. Modify therapy or monitor closely. Calcium decreases serum phosphate concentrations by binding dietary phosphate. Use alternatives if available. Calcium gluconate decreases the effectiveness of intravenous sodium phosphates by binding cations in the gastrointestinal tract. Modify therapy or monitor closely. Calcium decreases serum phosphate concentrations by binding dietary phosphate. Use alternatives if available. Dichlorphenamide and intravenous sodium phosphates both decrease serum potassium levels. Either drug can increase the toxicity of the other through pharmacodynamic synergy. Modify therapy or monitor closely. Both drugs can cause metabolic acidosis. Furosemide reduces the effectiveness of intravenous sodium phosphates by increasing renal clearance. Modify therapy or monitor closely. Furosemide lowers serum phosphate levels by enhancing renal excretion. Use alternatives if available. Magnesium citrate decreases the effectiveness of intravenous sodium phosphates by binding cations in the gastrointestinal tract. Modify therapy or monitor closely. Magnesium decreases serum phosphate concentrations by binding dietary phosphate. Use alternatives if available. Magnesium hydroxide also reduces the effectiveness of intravenous sodium phosphates through cation binding in the gastrointestinal tract. Modify therapy or monitor closely. Magnesium decreases serum phosphate concentrations by binding dietary phosphate. Use alternatives if available. Intravenous sodium phosphates may decrease the effectiveness of pseudoephedrine through an unknown mechanism. Use caution and monitor closely. Urinary excretion of indirect-acting alpha/beta agonists (e.g., pseudoephedrine) may increase when administered with urinary acidifying agents, resulting in lower serum concentrations. Voclosporin and intravenous sodium phosphates can mutually increase each other's toxicity through nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. Modify therapy or monitor closely. Co-administration with drugs associated with nephrotoxicity may increase the risk of acute and/or chronic nephrotoxicity. High concentrations of phosphorus may cause hypocalcemia and hypocalcemic tetany. Monitor calcium levels closely. Administer intravenous sodium phosphates slowly to avoid hypernatremia or hyperphosphatemia. Exercise caution in patients with severe renal or adrenal insufficiency due to the risk of sodium retention. Use with great care, if at all, in patients with conditions such as congestive heart failure, cirrhosis, or severe renal insufficiency, which are associated with sodium retention. Phosphorus and sodium are normal components of human milk. Decisions regarding administration during breastfeeding should consider the risk of infant exposure, the benefits of breastfeeding to the infant, and the benefits of therapy to the mother. Phosphorus plays a critical role in numerous biochemical functions, including metabolic and enzymatic reactions in nearly all organs and tissues. It influences calcium homeostasis, acid-base equilibrium, and renal hydrogen ion excretion. Sodium, the principal extracellular cation, is essential for regulating extracellular and intravascular volume. Sodium is excreted primarily through urine (90%) and feces (10%). Calcium and phosphorus are incompatible and will precipitate in most aqueous solutions. They may be mixed in some total parenteral nutrition (TPN) admixtures under specific conditions, such as composition, mixing order, pH, temperature, storage, and the type of calcium salt used. Consult a pharmacist for guidance. Do not administer unless the solution is clear and the seal is intact. Discard any unused portion. Administer intravenously only after dilution in a larger volume of fluid. Infuse slowly over 4–6 hours. Store at 20–25°C (68–77°F), with excursions permitted to 15–30°C (59–86°F). This product does not contain a bacteriostatic agent or other preservatives; discard any unused portion. In case of overdose, if serious symptoms such as loss of consciousness or difficulty breathing occur, call 911 immediately. Otherwise, contact a poison control center. U.S. residents can call 1-800-222-1222. Do not flush medications down the toilet or pour them into a drain unless instructed to do so.
